book.title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
book.author: Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson

confidence_note: Castor quote and the Criner, Florida and Dedge material come from chapter notes (Chapter 5) cross-checked against case records; the second-lab and vacate beat (f15) and Godschalk's later statement come from the case record, not the book, and are worded as such. The old text's survey of 200+ exonerees and its quoted rationalisations are not in the book and were dropped. The exact county is not named because the chapter notes and the case record disagree.
facts: Chapter 5 'Law and Disorder': district attorney Bruce Castor rejected a DNA result that cleared Bruce Godschalk, who had served fifteen years; police had recorded Godschalk's confession.
Asked for a scientific basis: 'I have no scientific basis. I know because I trust my detective and my tape-recorded confession.'
Case record: Castor's office sent the evidence to a second laboratory, which also excluded Godschalk; in February 2002 Castor asked a judge to vacate the convictions.
Texas: DNA from a young rape-murder victim did not match Roy Criner, the convicted man; prosecutor Michael McDougal said it meant the sperm found in her was not his.

Florida: after more than 130 DNA exonerations in fifteen years, prosecutors mounted a vigorous challenge to similar new cases; Wilton Dedge had to sue to get his evidence retested; prosecutors cited the state's interest in finality; he was exonerated and released.
Authors do not read the prosecutors as liars: 'I am good at this work' collides with 'I helped convict an innocent person', and cognitive dissonance plus self-justification explain which gives way.
scene_details: a retest the prisoner had to sue for
tension: A DNA result cleared a man after fifteen years and the prosecutor answered with a tape and his trust in a detective.
opening_idea: Open on the tape against the lab report, or on the Florida count, or the Texas sperm line; each language picks its own.

lessons.idea: Decide beforehand what evidence would change your mind.
lessons.anchor: Castor named no scientific basis, only trust in his detective and the tape.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A café owner writes down which result would make her switch suppliers before complaints arrive.

reflect_final: What evidence would have to turn up before you reversed a decision you are defending right now?

use_cases.situation: A team defends a plan before results are in.
use_cases.move: Cite the prosecutor holding to a tape over a DNA result, then write down which result would make the team drop the plan.

use_cases.situation: A friend shows you something suggesting you were wrong.
use_cases.move: Ask for a day before answering, and say you can feel yourself arguing.

use_cases.situation: A decision of yours is questioned.
use_cases.move: Write what you would see if you were wrong, now.

pocket_idea: Write down what would change your mind before the result arrives.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: DNA cleared a man after fifteen years; the DA trusted his detective and a tape.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Castor, the DNA, the tape, the authors' reading as dissonance rather than lying.
